lessons.title: Your first hockey question
lessons.objective: Start a conversation about hockey with someone new to the sport.

payload.title: Opening night chat
payload.setting: The new season starts tonight and she is texting you before puck drop.

exchanges.theirMessage: Puck drops tonight and {{team}} opens the season. I've been counting down for weeks.

replies.text: Who are you most excited to watch? I'm still learning who's who.
replies.theirResponse: Our new defenseman, honestly. I'll point him out.
replies.coachNote: Curious and honest about what you do not know yet.

replies.text: Cool. Who are they playing?
replies.theirResponse: Our division rival. It's always a good one.
replies.coachNote: Friendly and harmless, but it stays on the surface.

replies.text: Isn't hockey just guys skating around?
replies.theirResponse: Wow. Okay. Stick around and you'll see.
replies.coachNote: A joke at the sport's expense can land as a joke at her.

exchanges.theirMessage: You should watch the opener with me. I'll explain whatever you want.

replies.text: I'd love that. I'll bring snacks and a lot of questions.
replies.theirResponse: Perfect. Questions are the best part.
replies.coachNote: You said yes and promised curiosity, not expertise.

replies.text: Maybe, I'll see how my night goes.
replies.theirResponse: No pressure. The offer stands.
replies.coachNote: Polite, but it leaves her hanging.

replies.text: I already know hockey. I'll explain it to you.
replies.theirResponse: Um, okay. I've watched for twenty years.
replies.coachNote: Claiming knowledge you do not have costs you trust fast.

payload.closingNote: Be curious, be honest about what you do not know and say yes to her invitation.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: I don't know anything about hockey. Is it too late to start?

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: Not at all. Plenty of people start as adults. Want to learn it together?
options.explanation: Right. It is warm, true and it does not pretend you are an expert. Learning together is a great place to start.

options.text: Hockey is pretty hard. You might not get it.
options.explanation: It is discouraging and not true. Most people pick up the basics in a few games.

options.text: You could just watch and figure it out on your own.
options.explanation: It is not unkind, but it leaves her alone with it. An offer to learn together works better.

payload.translation: She is nervous about starting. Reassure her and offer to learn alongside her.

followUps.line: Want to watch a game and I'll ask questions too?
followUps.why: Offers a low-pressure, shared way in.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not have to be the expert. 'Let's learn it together' is honest and inviting.

payload.prompt: A beginner says she wants to learn hockey. Best first step?

options.text: Ask why she is interested.
Explain every rule right away.
Quiz her to see what she knows.

explanation.correct: Right. Her reason shapes what to teach first. A crush, a family tradition and a love of the speed all point to different starting places.
explanation.incorrect: Start with curiosity about why she cares. An avalanche of rules or a quiz makes it feel like homework.
explanation.sayThisLine: What got you interested in hockey?

payload.prompt: Telling a beginner 'hockey is complicated' encourages her.

explanation.correct: False. Warning someone off before they start discourages them. Lead with enthusiasm and start small.
explanation.incorrect: It backfires. Build her confidence with one simple thing, like the three periods, instead of a warning.
explanation.sayThisLine: Lead with enthusiasm. One small thing at a time.

payload.prompt: Match each conversation starter to why it works.

pairs.definition: Shows you care about her reason and tells you where to start.
Gives her a simple foundation instead of a pile of rules.
Builds trust. You do not need to be an expert to enjoy hockey.

explanation.summary: A good opening is about her, not about proving you know hockey.
explanation.sayThisLine: The best first question is about her. Everything else flows from there.

lessons.title: After a win
lessons.objective: Celebrate a win with genuine engagement and smart questions.

payload.title: A rookie's first goal
payload.setting: She texts you right after {{team}} wins on a young player's first NHL goal.

exchanges.theirMessage: Our rookie scored his first NHL goal and it was the game winner! I'm screaming.

replies.text: What a moment for him. Did the team grab the puck for him?
replies.theirResponse: They did! His parents were in the stands. I teared up.
replies.coachNote: You know the first-goal puck tradition, and you asked about the human side.

replies.text: Nice! Good for him.
replies.theirResponse: Thanks! It was great.
replies.coachNote: Warm, but it does not open the story.

replies.text: Only one goal? That's not much.
replies.theirResponse: It was the winner, though.
replies.coachNote: A deflating take on her big moment.

exchanges.theirMessage: And we just moved into a playoff spot.

replies.text: A playoff spot! Is it a wild card or a division spot?
replies.theirResponse: Wild card. It's tight, but I'll take it.
replies.coachNote: A specific question that shows you know how spots work.

replies.text: Cool, playoffs are fun.
replies.theirResponse: They really are!
replies.coachNote: Friendly but generic.

replies.text: It's only one win. It doesn't mean anything.
replies.theirResponse: Let me be happy for a minute.
replies.coachNote: Save the realism for later. Match her joy first.

payload.closingNote: Celebrate the moment, then ask the question only someone paying attention would ask.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We beat our biggest rival! I'm so pumped!

payload.question: What's a good follow-up question?

options.text: How did it feel to beat them? What was the key to winning?
options.explanation: Right. It matches her excitement and asks about the game itself, which is what she wants to relive.

options.text: Great win, but you'll probably lose to them next time.
options.explanation: It punctures her moment with a prediction nobody asked for.

options.text: Does this guarantee you make the playoffs?
options.explanation: It moves straight to math and skips the celebration she is living in.

payload.translation: A good follow-up honors her excitement and asks about the game, not the season math.

followUps.line: Was it close the whole way or did you pull away?
followUps.why: Explores the flow of the game.

followUps.line: Do you play them again soon?
followUps.why: Shows interest in the rivalry story.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know the game details. Asking her to tell you is better than guessing.

payload.prompt: After her team wins, which question shows you care about the game?

options.text: Who scored the game-winner, and how?
Did they score more than last game?
Was the score on the TV right?

explanation.correct: Right. Asking about the game-winner and how it happened invites the story she wants to tell.
explanation.incorrect: Skip the bookkeeping. The go-ahead goal and how it happened is the story fans want to tell.
explanation.sayThisLine: Who got the winner? Tell me about it.

payload.prompt: After her team wins, downplaying the victory is a smart move.

explanation.correct: False. Celebrate with her. Downplaying a win she loves makes her pull back.
explanation.incorrect: Match her energy. You can get into the standings math tomorrow.

lessons.title: After a loss
lessons.objective: React to a loss with empathy and thoughtful questions.

payload.title: A lead that got away
payload.setting: She texts you after {{team}} blew a two-goal lead in the third period.

exchanges.theirMessage: We were up two going into the third and lost in regulation. I'm sick.

replies.text: Brutal. A two-goal lead feels safe until it isn't. What changed in the third?
replies.theirResponse: They started pressing and we stopped skating.
replies.coachNote: Empathy first, then a question about the game.

replies.text: That's hockey.
replies.theirResponse: I know. It still hurts.
replies.coachNote: True, but it shuts the door on the feeling.

replies.text: You should have known a two-goal lead isn't safe.
replies.theirResponse: Thanks for the hindsight.
replies.coachNote: Never pile on when she is hurting.

exchanges.theirMessage: I think I'm done watching for a few days.

replies.text: Take a night off. I'll check in tomorrow and we can talk about the next one.
replies.theirResponse: That sounds nice. Thanks for getting it.
replies.coachNote: You gave her space and a warm plan.

replies.text: Come on, don't be dramatic.
replies.theirResponse: It's not dramatic. It's my team.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing her feelings is the fastest way to lose the thread.

replies.text: Okay.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah.
replies.coachNote: Polite but flat.

payload.closingNote: After a loss, empathy first and curiosity second. Let her decide how much to talk.

payload.prompt: She is upset about a loss. What should you do first?

options.text: Remind her of the team's earlier wins.
Show empathy and listen to what she is feeling.
Try to cheer her up with jokes.

explanation.correct: Right. Empathy first. Once she feels heard she will be ready to talk about the game itself.
explanation.incorrect: Comfort comes before analysis or jokes. Let her feel it, then ask a real question.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a tough one. I'm sorry.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: I've never been so mad at a team. They played awful in the third.

payload.question: What's a good response?

options.text: They looked out of gas. Was it a back-to-back?
options.explanation: Right. A back-to-back means two games in two nights, a common reason for a tired third period. You showed empathy and asked a real question.

options.text: Yeah, they're just not good.
options.explanation: It dumps on her team while she is already hurting.

options.text: At least you're not a fan of a worse team.
options.explanation: It minimizes her disappointment instead of sharing it.

payload.translation: She is venting about a collapse. Ask about context, like schedule or injuries, instead of judging.

followUps.line: Do they usually fade in the third?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you do not know the cause, ask. Guessing out loud can sound like a know-it-all.

payload.prompt: Match each loss response to how it lands.

pairs.definition: Validates her feelings without trying to fix them.
A real question that keeps her talking.
Backfires because it minimizes her disappointment.

explanation.summary: After a loss, lead with empathy. Questions come after she feels heard.

lessons.title: When the ref ruins the night
lessons.objective: Talk about a controversial call without dismissing her frustration.

payload.title: Four minutes of kill
payload.setting: She texts during the second period after a call against {{team}}.

exchanges.theirMessage: They gave our guy a double minor for high-sticking. Four minutes! It was an accident.

replies.text: Four minutes usually means someone got cut. Was there blood?
replies.theirResponse: Yes, a cut on the cheek. Still, it wasn't on purpose.
replies.coachNote: You know a double minor often comes from an injury, and you asked instead of guessing.

replies.text: Ugh, that's a lot.
replies.theirResponse: It is. Four minutes down a man.
replies.coachNote: Sympathetic, but it does not show what you know.

replies.text: Refs ruin every game.
replies.theirResponse: Not every game. Just this call.
replies.coachNote: Blaming every ref sounds lazy.

exchanges.theirMessage: We killed all four minutes though!

replies.text: Four minutes with no goal against is huge. Who was the best penalty killer?
replies.theirResponse: Our goalie, then the top defense pair. It swung the game.
replies.coachNote: You spotted the turning point and asked for a name.

replies.text: Good for you.
replies.theirResponse: Thanks!
replies.coachNote: Kind, but flat.

replies.text: So was it even a real penalty then?
replies.theirResponse: It was. We just survived it.
replies.coachNote: Questioning the call right after her comeback misses her point.

payload.closingNote: Validate the frustration first. Then a rule-aware question shows you are paying attention.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Our goal got waved off for goalie interference. That was a joke!

payload.question: How would you respond?

options.text: Goalie interference is one of the most argued calls. What did you see happen?
options.explanation: Right. The rule is judged by the officials, so fans and referees disagree a lot. Asking what she saw is respectful and curious.

options.text: Yeah, the ref made a bad call.
options.explanation: You are taking a side without knowing what happened.

options.text: Don't worry, refs get most calls right.
options.explanation: It dismisses her frustration when she just wants to vent.

payload.translation: She is angry about a disallowed goal. Goalie interference calls are a common source of arguments.

followUps.line: Was he in the crease, or just nearby?
followUps.why: Shows you know the rule has a geography to it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you did not see the play, say so. Asking what happened beats pretending to know.

payload.prompt: When she is angry about a penalty call, defending the referee is wise.

explanation.correct: False. Right now she needs you on her side. Defending the ref makes her feel unheard.
explanation.incorrect: Validate her frustration first. There is time for the ref debate later, if ever.
explanation.sayThisLine: That sounds so frustrating. What did you see?

payload.prompt: Why is goalie interference argued about so often?

options.text: Everyone agrees on what it is, and officials never err.
There is a gray area between incidental contact and impairing the goalie.
It never affects the outcome of a game.

explanation.correct: Right. Judging whether an attacker impaired the goalie is subjective, so good-faith disagreements happen constantly.
explanation.incorrect: It is argued because the judgment is subjective. Fans and officials can look at the same contact and disagree.
explanation.sayThisLine: Where does contact end and interference begin? Fans argue about it all the time.

lessons.title: The goalie stole it
lessons.objective: Talk about a dominant goalie performance with the right stats.

payload.title: The backup's big night
payload.setting: She texts after {{team}}'s backup goalie gets an unexpected start.

exchanges.theirMessage: Our backup goalie started tonight and he stopped a penalty shot. Nobody expected that.

replies.text: A penalty shot save! That's one-on-one with no help. How was he the rest of the night?
replies.theirResponse: Twenty-eight saves on twenty-nine shots. The starter was resting.
replies.coachNote: You know a penalty shot is a one-on-one, and you asked a follow-up.

replies.text: Backups usually aren't that good.
replies.theirResponse: Well, he was tonight.
replies.coachNote: Dismissive of a goalie she just cheered for.

replies.text: Lucky save.
replies.theirResponse: It wasn't luck. He read the shooter.
replies.coachNote: Calling it luck undercuts her excitement.

exchanges.theirMessage: The coach might ride him in the next game too.

replies.text: If he's hot, does the coach stick with him, or does the starter come back?
replies.theirResponse: That's the big question. The starter's been good too.
replies.coachNote: You named a real coaching dilemma.

replies.text: Whatever the coach wants.
replies.theirResponse: Fair enough.
replies.coachNote: Shrugging gives her nothing to talk about.

replies.text: Never switch goalies. It's bad luck.
replies.theirResponse: That's not how it works.
replies.coachNote: Bluffing a rule you do not know can sound like faking.

payload.closingNote: Ask what the goalie faced and what comes next. Specific questions beat big claims.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The goalie was the only reason we stayed in the game.

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: That's when great goaltending shows up. Did the team finally help him out?
options.explanation: Right. You credit the goalie and ask whether the skaters backed him up with goals.

options.text: So the team was terrible?
options.explanation: It turns her praise into criticism of her team.

options.text: Goalies only matter for shutouts.
options.explanation: Goalies matter on every save, and a game can hinge on one.

payload.translation: She is saying the goalie saved the day. Celebrate that and ask about the rest of the team.

followUps.line: How many shots did he face?
followUps.why: Puts a number on the pressure.

followUps.line: Did someone score late to get him the win?
followUps.why: Explores whether the team came through.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need stats memorized. A shot count question is enough to sound engaged.

payload.prompt: What does a .950 save percentage mean?

options.text: The goalie stopped 95 percent of the shots he faced.
The goalie played 95 percent of the game.
The goalie made 95 saves.

explanation.correct: Right. Save percentage is saves divided by shots, so .950 means he stopped 95 of every 100. For a single game that is excellent.
explanation.incorrect: Save percentage is saves divided by shots faced. .950 means 95 out of every 100 shots were stopped.
explanation.sayThisLine: A .950 night is elite. He stopped almost everything.

payload.prompt: A goalie who faces 40 shots must have played brilliantly.

explanation.correct: False. Forty shots only tells you how busy he was. What matters is how many he stopped, which is his save percentage.
explanation.incorrect: Shots faced shows workload, not quality. A goalie can face 40 shots and play poorly or great depending on how many went in.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forty shots is a lot. How many did he stop?

lessons.title: Playoff nerves
lessons.objective: Talk about playoff intensity and matchup strategy.

payload.title: Down three games to one
payload.setting: She texts while {{team}} is trailing in a playoff series.

exchanges.theirMessage: We're down 3-1 in the series. I can't even breathe.

replies.text: That's rough, but teams have come back from 3-1. What does yours need to change?
replies.theirResponse: Score first and protect the net. If we get the lead we can do this.
replies.coachNote: Honest hope, and a real question.

replies.text: Sorry. It's probably over.
replies.theirResponse: Wow, thanks for the pep talk.
replies.coachNote: Honest doesn't have to mean hopeless.

replies.text: Sorry.
replies.theirResponse: Thanks.
replies.coachNote: Kind, but it gives her nothing to grab.

exchanges.theirMessage: At least Game 5 is at home.

replies.text: Home ice for Game 5. Does your building give the team a boost?
replies.theirResponse: Oh, it's deafening. Visiting teams can barely hear each other.
replies.coachNote: You linked the game to the crowd.

replies.text: Home ice doesn't matter much.
replies.theirResponse: It matters to me.
replies.coachNote: Even if true, it lands cold right now.

replies.text: Okay.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah.
replies.coachNote: Flat.

payload.closingNote: Acknowledge the stress, stay honest and ask one good question about what comes next.

payload.prompt: What does 'best-of-seven' mean in the playoffs?

options.text: The first team to win four games wins the series.
Both teams play seven games no matter what.
The team with the best regular-season record wins.

explanation.correct: Right. First to four wins takes the series, and it can end in four, five, six or seven games.
explanation.incorrect: Best-of-seven means the first team to four wins takes the series. The series stops the moment someone gets there.
explanation.sayThisLine: Best-of-seven means first to four wins.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We lost Game 1. Is the series over?

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: No. It's a best-of-seven. One loss doesn't end it.
options.explanation: Right. A team needs four wins, so one loss leaves plenty of series. It is a calm, accurate reassurance.

options.text: Yeah, nobody comes back from 0-1.
options.explanation: Teams win series after losing Game 1 all the time.

options.text: Yes, you need to win the next four in a row.
options.explanation: That is not how it works. A team needs four total wins, not four in a row.

payload.translation: One loss in a best-of-seven is not decisive. She is nervous and needs a calm, accurate answer.

followUps.why: Explores whether the team was competitive.

followUps.line: What does your team need to change for Game 2?
followUps.why: Focuses on adjustments instead of panic.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You only need the format: first to four. Everything else is her territory.

payload.prompt: Match each playoff term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The team with the better record hosts Games 1, 2, 5 and 7.
The winner-take-all game when a series is tied 3-3.
A lower seed or underdog beating the favorite.

explanation.summary: These three terms show up constantly in playoff talk and explain why series feel so tense.
explanation.sayThisLine: Home ice matters. The deciding game at home is huge.

lessons.title: Watching a game together
lessons.objective: Explain the game live without condescension while she asks questions.

payload.title: Intermission chat
payload.setting: You are watching a game together and the first period just ended.

exchanges.theirMessage: We outshot them 18 to 7 and it's still 1-1. What's going on?

replies.text: Eighteen to seven is a lot. Are those good shots, or mostly from far out?
replies.theirResponse: Mostly from the outside. Their goalie has an easy night.
replies.coachNote: You asked about shot quality, which is the heart of it.

replies.text: So we're winning?
replies.theirResponse: Not quite. It's tied.
replies.coachNote: An honest question, but it skips past what she said.

replies.text: Shots don't matter. Only goals.
replies.theirResponse: They kind of do, but I see what you mean.
replies.coachNote: A sweeping claim when you are still learning.

exchanges.theirMessage: What do you think we should do in the second period?

replies.text: Honestly I'm still learning, but maybe get more shots to the middle of the ice? What do you think?
replies.theirResponse: Yes! Get to the slot and screen the goalie.
replies.coachNote: Honest, curious and you handed the question back to her.

replies.text: Play harder!
replies.theirResponse: Ha, always good advice.
replies.coachNote: Safe, but it adds nothing.

replies.text: Change the lines and fire the coach.
replies.theirResponse: Whoa, okay, coach.
replies.coachNote: Loud confidence you have not earned is a fake-expert move.

payload.closingNote: It is fine to say 'I'm still learning'. Asking her opinion is better than bluffing your own.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Why did they just blow the whistle? Nothing happened.

payload.question: How would you respond?

options.text: Not sure yet. Let's see what the replay shows. Could be offside, icing or a penalty.
options.explanation: Right. You are honest about not knowing and name real possibilities. Hockey has several common reasons for a whistle.

options.text: It was definitely a penalty.
options.explanation: That is a guess stated as fact. If it turns out to be icing, you have just bluffed.

options.text: You'll learn what it means over time.
options.explanation: It is condescending and does not answer her question.

payload.translation: She spotted a whistle and does not know why. Admit you are not sure and investigate together.

followUps.line: Did the puck go over the glass?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: 'Not sure yet, let's find out' is a great answer. Fans respect it more than a bluff.

payload.prompt: When watching together, you should explain everything before she asks.

explanation.correct: False. Let her ask. She learns what she wants to know, and you avoid talking over the game.
explanation.incorrect: Answer her questions and let her lead. She will enjoy it more than a running lecture.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask me anything. I'll give you the short version.

payload.prompt: She asks what a rule means mid-play. Best approach?

options.text: Explain it in detail, with every exception.
Give a short answer and keep watching.
Say you'll explain it after the game.

explanation.correct: Right. A short answer helps her follow the play, and you can go deeper at the next intermission.
explanation.incorrect: A long lecture makes you miss the game together. Answer briefly and save the detail for intermission.
explanation.sayThisLine: Short version: they can't do that. More at the break.

lessons.title: Ask about her hockey story
lessons.objective: Ask meaningful questions about her personal connection to hockey.

payload.title: The girl who played defense
payload.setting: She mentions in passing that she used to play hockey herself.

exchanges.theirMessage: I played hockey as a kid, all the way through high school, before I stopped.

replies.text: You played?! What position? Do you miss it?
replies.theirResponse: Defense! I loved blocking shots. I don't miss the 5 a.m. practices, though.
replies.coachNote: Two warm questions about her, not the sport.

replies.text: That's neat.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, it was fun.
replies.coachNote: Friendly, but it does not open the story.

replies.text: Really? I never pictured you as a hockey player.
replies.theirResponse: Well, I was. Women's hockey has been around a long time.
replies.coachNote: Assuming who plays hockey can land as dismissive. Ask, do not assume.

exchanges.theirMessage: I still keep my old skates in the closet.

replies.text: Would you ever lace them up again? I'd love to try, though I'd be terrible.
replies.theirResponse: Ha! I'll teach you. Bring a helmet.
replies.coachNote: A playful, honest offer that invites you into her world.

replies.text: Skates are cool.
replies.theirResponse: They are.
replies.coachNote: Says nothing new.

replies.text: You should sell them.
replies.theirResponse: They're not for sale. They're memories.
replies.coachNote: Practical advice misses the feeling in her voice.

payload.closingNote: Her story is personal. Ask about the moments, the position and the feelings.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: My favorite player got traded and I'm still not over it.

payload.question: How would you follow up?

options.text: How long had he been your favorite? What made him special to you?
options.explanation: Right. You honor the loss and invite her to tell you why he mattered.

options.text: There are plenty of other players on the team.
options.explanation: It brushes aside something she genuinely feels.

options.text: At least he went to a good team.
options.explanation: It is a silver lining she did not ask for.

payload.translation: Honor the loss. Ask about the connection, not why she should move on.

followUps.line: Did you get to see him play a lot?
followUps.why: Explores how much she followed him.

followUps.line: Do you still follow him at the new team?
followUps.why: Shows the fan bond can outlast a trade.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know the trade details. Asking about him is what matters.

payload.prompt: Which question best opens her hockey story?

options.text: How much do you know about hockey?
What's your favorite hockey memory?
Do you follow the standings?

explanation.correct: Right. A memory question invites a story, and stories are where her love of the sport lives.
explanation.incorrect: Questions about what she knows or the standings feel like a test. A memory feels like an invitation.

payload.prompt: Match each question type to what it reveals.

pairs.definition: Opens up her personal story and the feelings tied to it.
Gets a number but not why hockey matters to her.
Explores the people behind her fandom.

explanation.summary: The best questions connect to her story, not just hockey facts.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask about the people, the moments and the feelings.
